U4I0) NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS CALL FOR SUMMIT MEETING BETWEEN AMERICAN AND RUSSIAN LEADERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 16 1 said the following in the House:
This fear and anxiety of nuclear annihilation comes not from delivery systems but from nuclear warheads which have multiplied unchecked in an almost crazy, insane, mad progression which must be checked and reversed. The task is to do away with nuclear warheads and their deployment. Summit level meetings are vital and mandatory.
The recent announcement by General Secretary Andropov to base negotiations on warheads rather than just missiles is an encouraging development.
On November 17 and again on November 24, 1982,1 moved motions in the House calling for unanimous support for a summit meeting within 18 months between President Reagan and General Secretary Andropov to strengthen nuclear detente and initiate the process for nuclear arms stabilization and eventual reduction. Twice the House would not give its unanimous consent. I hope it has changed its mind.
Since then Canadians were pleased to know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pleaded with President Reagan to hold a summit meeting. Everyone in the House should also plead and support unanimously the need for such a summit meeting. I hope the Government will put forth such a motion. I am prepared to circulate a petition for signature by all Hon. Members and Senators, supporting a summit meeting.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), afraid to debate in the House of Commons the Cruise missile issue, has said in a planted letter to newspapers that Canadians who oppose Cruise missile tests are anti-American. Does the Prime Minister not know that the American people themselves are increasingly opposed to the continuation of the nuclear arms madness, that the House of Representatives has just passed, 278 to 149, a resolution calling for a mutual, verifiable nuclear freeze? Canadians who oppose the further escalation of the nuclear arms race and Canada's participation in it by testing the Cruise, do so in concert with the majority of Americans. Are the majority of Americans anti-American?
The Prime Minister says we must test nuclear weapons as payment for the American defence umbrella. Yet the Reagan strategy for a massive nuclear arms build-up, space based weapons, and winnable nuclear war, and the inevitable Soviet countering moves, is no umbrella. It is the shadowy Horsemen of the Apocalypse that Americans themselves are rejecting.
It is the Prime Minister, not Canadians, who is being hypocritical on this issue, saying that Cruise missile testing
will not be agreed to until progress has been measured at the Geneva talks, when we all know that he has given assurances to the Reagan administration that testing will go ahead. Or is this planted letter an attempt to soften up Canadians for Canada's next leap in the nuclear arms race?

speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must first point out that there has been no request made of Canada to test the Cruise. There is, therefore, no support for the testing of the Cruise. It has not been asked of us and, therefore, we have not given an answer.
I just wish to correct the end of the question. The substance of the question is to ask why do we not support the peace movement now rather than say we should make sure that there is an answer within NATO against the SS-20. It seems to me there may be an honest disagreement there. To me it is not illogical to use the possibility of deploying the Cruise and the Pershing II to get the Soviets to withdraw all or some of their SS-20s. The argument, of course, rests on whether the SS-20s were necessary or whether they were just an escalation by the Soviets. If they are, as NATO holds, a needless escalation by the Soviets, the problem for the NATO force is how can we get the Soviets to de-escalate. There the proof of the pudding is in the results.
The two-track strategy adopted by NATO in 1979 has led Secretary Andropov twice to propose reductions of the SS-20, once in December and once just a week ago. Therefore it seems to me that we cannot condemn in advance any potential deployment by NATO of a European Euromissile if the result of it continues to be as it is now, a reduction in the number of these SS-20s.

subtopic: VIEWS OF FORMER HEAD OF U.S. CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY
VIEWS OF FORMER HEAD OF U.S. CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister, who has followed the literature on this with some care, I understand, knows perfectly well that whenever there is an escalation it is always justified by either side in terms of being a step required to get the opponent to come to terms with regard to negotiations or to de-escalate on the other side. I see the Prime Minister nodding to that. In short, it is
May 10, 1983

the kind of argument in which there is no empirical evidence to support strongly one way or the other.
The Prime Minister is not an expert in this field, nor am I. The former head of the CIA wrote an article last week in opposition to the Cruise. He can hardly be called anti-American. He said:
The Soviets are certainly not "superior" to the United States in any meaningful way today ... The present American retaliation potential is absolute.
Considering that Mr. Colby says that in terms of the present weaponry, does this not cause the Prime Minister to question his own judgment? Does it not pose for him the necessity of Canada joining with the U.S. Congress in calling for a freeze at this time?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VIEWS OF FORMER HEAD OF U.S. CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE AGENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are several questions contained in that. The actions of the U.S. Congress, or indeed of Americans who are arguing against President Reagan's over-all nuclear policy, are one thing. I am not supporting President Reagan's over-all nuclear policy. It is not my purpose to do so. I have not been asked to do so. What I am supporting is NATO's two-track policy. That can be accepted even if we agree with some of the statements quoted by my hon. friend.
I have not seen that statement by the former director of the CIA, but some of the quotes would be acceptable to me in the sense that there is certainly power of overkill in the United States now and power of overkill in the Soviet Union now. In other words, either side is in a position to destroy not only the enemy but probably a large part of humanity as well.
I do not know, Madam Speaker, what kibitzing is coming from the NDP. If they want a rational answer they should listen to me.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister has just said that the United States is in a position to wipe out the Soviet Union. Of course the Soviet Union is now in a position to wipe out the United States, and both are potentially in a position to wipe out mankind. If that is the case, I should like to know the logic of the two-track position. Why is it necessary to go ahead with the Cruise? Does it not make much more sense for Canada to act as a peaceful power, to take serious steps to bring about nuclear disarmament in the world, instead of contributing to its escalation in the opposite direction?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Yes, it makes eminent good sense. I hope we are acting as a peaceful power and a power that is seeking the eventual reduction of nuclear arms. That does not contradict my previous assertion that both super powers can destroy each other. That is the rationale of the deterrence that each side holds and which has deterred nuclear war since both sides have had the nuclear power.
Oral Questions
The Cruise, the Pershing II, and the SS-20s are a completely different argument. What NATO is attempting to do is answer a theatre nuclear arm, the SS-20. We are saying that in so far as the survival of the United States the survival of the Soviet Union are concerned, both have cause to fear each other and therefore they are unlikely to start fighting against each other. But what is to prevent the Soviet Union if it wishes to start a limited war in Europe with SS-20s? I do not know how limited it would be, but we know they have 300 or 400 SS-20s, each with three nuclear warheads which are capable of destroying all of western Europe. We know that as a fact.
How does NATO, which includes countries in Europe, counter that? It can only counter it by saying to the United States, "Well, if the Soviet Union attacks western Europe, you send off your big ones and destroy all of humanity."
Does it not make sense, Madam Speaker, in Europe to try to have a counter threat to the Soviet Union so that it will not use its SS-20s on western Europe, any more than it would use its ICBMs on the United States of America?

Mr. Speaker, prior to the recess I was pointing out that the Government has been borrowing money during this session of Parliament at the
May 10, 1983

rate of some $68,833,482 per day, an amount, over this Parliament, of $77.3 billion in extra borrowing. I should like to continue my remarks and point out how the Government has absolutely wasted at least $1.3 billion of that in concert with the Conservative-Social Credit Government of British Columbia on a boondoggle called northeast coal. That misin-vestment, that misallocation of financial priorities has already made its devastating effect clear by the loss at this point of 460 permanent coal mining jobs in south-eastern British Columbia.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The noise level in the House is too high. Would Hon. Members please hold their conversations outside.

About a week and a half ago BCTV carried a program showing the effect of the Government's policies in terms of putting working people at each other's throats even today in northern British Columbia. It showed a disgusting scene of workers coming in from the Provinces of Alberta, Ontario and Quebec to northern British Columbia, taking jobs away from British Columbians with Alberta contracts because the Conservatives and Liberals in the Social Credit Government of British Columbia had manipulated the Labour Code to open those jobs to non-union people. Workers from outside the Province with outside contracts were stealing B.C. jobs at the cheap rate of $7 per hour. They had to rent tarpaper shacks for their families, not good construction camps, but tarpaper shacks, at $450 per month for families sometimes with four children.
One worker who was interviewed on the program said that with $7 per hour wages, at the rate he was being charged for rent he would be better off to go back to Alberta and draw Unemployment Insurance benefits. The TV reporter asked him why he did not quit, and he said that if he quit he would not get Unemployment Insurance, and besides, in the hobo jungle just down the road there were ten guys willing to battle and replace everyone who had a job. The cameras went down to the hobo jungle. Some of us never dreamed that in this part of the twentieth century we would see such pictures again. It was right out of "Grapes of Wrath".
That is the kind of stupid, insane policy that the Government is fostering by churning out $1.3 billion in public moneys along with its Conservative cohorts in the Socred Government of British Columbia. It is just shovelling it out by the carload in order to give contracts to their friends, even though, because of declining demand which was forecast and declining prices which were forecast, the federal Government and the provincial Government of B.C. had some airy-fairy figures drawn out of a never-never land on which they based the $1.3 billion subsidy to that development.
Already 460 people in southeastern British Columbia coalfields have been laid off because neither the price nor the demand are sufficient for the coal that we already produce with existing rail facilities and existing port facilities. This is a suicidal policy. It is an example of how that bunch over there has thrown away billions and billions of public money. When it comes to a choice between investing in and assisting established communities and groups of people versus building new pyramids somewhere in areas that do not have an existing
Borrowing Authority
population, those people over there and their allies in the provincial Government of British Columbia will always choose to build new empires and leave people in existing communities to rot. No one knows why.
The Sun in Vancouver of April 21 carried an article by a Mr. Halvorson, a Vancouver mining consultant, in which he said:
The B.C. government, through that subsidy, created competition to an existing business, may cost people their jobs, and perhaps destroy the owners' investment.
So, by building with public money an alternative to the production and transport facilities we already have in the southeast, they are not only throwing away workers' jobs there but destroying the return on the private investment that already existed in southeastern British Columbia. They are doing that at the expense of the public purse. The article continues:
In the northeast coal project the provincial government is subsidizing two new coal mines into production through massive investment in railways and other infrastructure. Those mines will sell coal into an oversupplied Japanese market in direct competition to mines that already exist in southeastern B.C. There is little doubt that serious job loss, and even mine closures, could occur in the southeast over the next two year period.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker. It has already started to happen even without the northeast project coming on stream. Meanwhile, the people in northeastern B.C. are not even getting the temporary advantages of decent jobs at decent pay.
The contractors of northeastern B.C. are not getting the temporary advantages either. Because of the meddling of the Labour Relations Board, jobs are going to contractors from outside the Province. What kind of insanity leads to that kind of policy?
This is not the only area in which the federal Government continues to wastefully churn out public money. British Columbia is not the only place. Every time the federal Government decides to give some minimal cost-of-living increases to pensioners across the country, what happens? We see provincial Governments not only pocketing those increases but dipping further into the pockets of ordinary pensioners, ripping them off to fatten their own coffers at federal Government expense. When are those people over there going to smarten up and tell some of those Tory and Socred Provinces that they cannot just steal public money, and they cannot steal out of the pockets of pensioners in order to make themselves look better on the books.
About a week and a half ago a Mr. and Mrs. Rhodes from my constituency, dropped into my office and showed me their last cheques. The federal Government in its Old Age Security payment had given them each an extra $2.34. That is a good policy. People should have payments to keep pace. However, at the very same time, their supplemental cheque from the provincial Government of British Columbia was cut by $3.00 a month each. The federal Government gave them four dollars and the Province took away six dollars. In some cases the

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
amount which the Province stole from those people was up to $50 a month per couple. The federal Goverment is allowing that to happen. What kind of agreement does it have with the Provinces? What kind of misplaced trust does it have in Tories and Socreds that it keeps on handing money over to them to stick in their own pockets?
About the only Government that I know of which has a worse financial record of getting deeper and deeper into debt at public expense than this Government in Ottawa, is the provincial Government in Victoria. Eight years ago it had an accumulated debt of some $4 billion which was spread over 100 years of Governments of all political stripes. That has more than trebled in just the last eight years. It is a record which almost makes the miserable record of the federal Government look good. That is the kind of wastage we are seeing at public expense continually.
Surely it is time, Mr. Speaker, for some new system of priorities. If the Government is going to go into debt, let it go into debt to create work and not simply to put people on welfare for years and years, not simply to pass on contracts to its friends, which is the only motivation we can think of for the northeast coal subsidy because it is going to devastate existing communities. We just cannot picture any other motivation. If Government wants to borrow, if it wants to use its existing financial capacity to build new industries, it must work out arrangements with some of our trading partners and, if we are going to sell resources and commit resources on a long-term basis, we must get something in return. We must have assurance that some of the facilities which will service these industries will be built in this country, with this country's labour and with this country's trained people. That would be a valid expenditure. It is time, Mr. Speaker, to put an end to the Government's just shovelling money out of the public bucket into its friends' pockets. Unfortunately, that is all that we have seen happening over the last number of years.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-151. This Bill seeks authority to borrow an additional $14.7 billion. To date, the Government has come to Parliament seven times in this session to seek more borrowing authority. In fact, the projected financial requirements of the Government between 1983-84 and 1986-87 total some $93 billion. This would indicate that Parliament is in for a steady stream of large borrowing Bills over the next few years. There are at least four distinct economic costs to continuing deficit financing of this magnitude. First, there is the ever-growing interest burden. This year interest on the national debt cost an estimated $17.6 billion, or the equivalent of $1,700 per taxpayer.
The second cost is the loss of fiscal flexibility. In the past the Government had the option of undertaking costly and significant fiscal measures to spur recovery. Today, Mr. Speaker, there is virtually no room remaining in which to manoeuvre.
The third cost is that the productive private sector when endeavouring to borrow is crowded out, and this is causing interest rates to rise. In the 1982 calendar year, federal Government borrowing accounted for 51 per cent of the net new security issues placed in Canada. If there was less federal Government borrowing, there would certainly be less demand for money and interest rates would be lower.
The fourth cost, Mr. Speaker, is one of confidence. The investment community does not trust a Government which continues to live so far beyond its means. They do not want to hold a currency which continues to be debased by excessive Government borrowing. As a consequence, our dollar is at a low ebb, thus driving up the cost of living in Canada. As the Government attempts to support the dollar, our job-creating capital has gone elsewhere.
By way of comparison between today's expenditures and those of 1968-69, when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office, I wish to place on the record the total spending for that year as taken from the book entitled, "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent" as it was reported by the then President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. C. M. Drury. It is an amazing little document. I have kept copies of it in my files, Mr. Speaker. In this report, the total listed for all functions of Government in 1968-69 amounted to $10,767 million. That is truly amazing. We were then a nation of some 20 million people. We have grown slowly in population to 25 million, but spending on a public accounts basis has grown for this year to a total of $90 billion, an increase of some 555 per cent. The reasons behind this fiasco are well documented. For example, the Auditor General of Canada, Mr. Dye, comments as follows in his Report:
The commitment for $1.7 billion to Petro-Canada by the department, without commensurate responsibility, raises serious concerns.
In an appendix to his report, Mr. Dye also noted other deficiencies: inadequate management controls in overpayments totalling $285.3 million under four major energy programs by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources; the Department of Public Works failed to recover expenditures from Canada Post Corporation of $61 million; during fiscal 1981, the Unemployment Insurance Commission is estimated to have made overpayments of $178 million, and the list goes on, page after page.
We are speaking today about a vast expenditure of money. Some of it undoubtedly will be well spent. Unfortunately, however, I fear that a large percentage of the amount listed in the Bill before the House will be wasted or spent frivolously on so-called make-work projects. These projects do not necessarily improve the infrastructure of Canada, nor do they give meaningful or long-term employment to our people.
I believe it is way past the time when we should be giving recognition to some salient facts, and plan accordingly for some meaningful Canadian development. For example, Canada is one of the major trading nations of the world. Everyone seems to know that, Mr. Speaker, but the Government. Canada is also a major deep sea shipping nation, but not
May 10, 1983

everyone is aware of that particular fact. Here we are, a major deep sea trading nation, and yet we do not have a Canadian merchant marine. We have relied for years on being able to buy the shipping services we need in the marketplace. We are paying out more than $3 billion annually to foreign shipping lines for their services, while our unemployment rolls exceed
1.5	million people at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. This simply does not make any sense, Mr. Speaker, at least not to me. That is a lot of service, and the practice of buying it abroad derives directly from the current Canadian marine policy of depending on the world market to provide bottoms for carrying Canadian goods overseas. It is a policy which has satisfied our needs up to this point, but whether or not it will prove adequate for our future needs is open to question.
I say this, Sir, because our present policy is cast in doubt by a number of developments in the world of international shipping. Neither does it seem at all prudent at this moment to depend on the international shipping world to provide for Canadian concerns in our northern areas. Nor should we assume that the marine policies we depend on today will enable us tomorrow adequately to cope with problems arising from development of our varied and invaluable offshore resources. We have been able to rely on the free market for deep sea shipping because of a world-wide surplus of vessels has made it possible until now to buy shipping services at very good rates. However, economic, technological and political developments may soon reduce the size of the free market fleet on which we depend. Growth in the world economy, slow though it may be at the moment, will gradually reduce the available surplus of shipping capacity. Furthermore, much of the surplus capacity swinging at anchor today, as we say in Atlantic Canada, while shipowners wait for the market to sort itself out, may never sail again. They may never sail again! They may be so outmoded in terms of fuel efficiency and pollution control by the time world markets strengthen again that they will have become obsolete. This is the danger we face. The world surplus in shipping capacity is, in this respect, more apparent than it is real.
In addition, political developments may reduce the size of the free-market fleet on which current Canadian marine policy depends for its effectiveness. We could find before the end of this decade that Canada cannot as readily obtain, as it does today, ships to carry at competitive rates Nova Scotia's apples to Britain, or New Brunswick timber or lumber to Scotland, or Prince Edward Island's potatoes to Venezuela. The issue, Sir, is a bottom-line issue, it is a pocketbook issue.
I say to you, Sir, and through you to the Government, that anything which impairs the ability of a trading nation to sell its goods has potentially grave implications for the health of its national economy. In such a context the limitations of current national marine policy are readily perceived. These limitations also become obvious the moment the problem of exerting effective and necessary control over Arctic and offshore development is addressed.
We will likely see large-scale commercial shipping invade the Arctic before the end of this decade, Mr. Speaker, since
Borrowing Authority
Canada has proven hydrocarbon reserves in the high North. I was in Frobisher Bay, for example, only last year and I was informed that drilling operations at that time were being carried out in Davis Strait. However, Canada's position in its Arctic waters is that it has sovereign control. Now, Sir, in theory this means ships moving in the region, in particular the Northwest Passage, will be subject to Canadian regulation and control. United States interests, however, reject the notion of Canadian sovereignty over the Passage and they claim it as an international waterway in which all shipping should have access. But the reality of the situation is that we simply do not have adequate means to assert our authority over the North.
Unfortunately, our current national marine policy is not directed toward encouraging development in Canada of the marine technologies which would allow us to exploit fully our opportunities in the North or cope with the problems of sovereignty there, any more than it is geared to deal with the opportunities and problems associated with our offshore resource development. Our offshore resources afford us opportunities which extend well beyond catching fish, well beyond pumping oil. We have a chance to develop here and now in Canada world class technical and ocean engineering skills. We have a moment in time in which to begin building technologies and services which ultimately we can export as readily as we export anything else that we make in this country. But the time to sieze that moment, Sir, is now. We cannot fritter away this time while offshore resource development is in its infancy. The time to seize that moment is now not later when other patterns of satisfying those needs have established themselves.
Beyond all that, we need to develop such skills and technologies at home in order to safeguard our interests in actually harvesting offshore resources. The issue is too vital, I submit, to be left to others. No one else will care as much as we do about whether or not Canadian fish and Canadian oil are safely exploited, Sir, in the same waters and at the same time. We need to develop the means to control our own offshore expansion. No one should for a moment imagine that either offshore development or the controls and technologies associated with it can mature in a context other than one established in larger measure by a national marine policy.
It is not hard today, when you start talking about this matter of a national marine policy, to find yourself dealing with an amazing array of issues. The shipbuilders, the ship repairers, ship suppliers, marine unions, all legitimately have something to say on this particular subject. Up to this point we have had a marine policy in this country which has served the nation if not the industry very well. But circumstances, Sir, are changing. There are forces loose in the world of international shipping which may affect the way in which we shall conduct international trade. There are problems associated with Arctic and offshore resource development which require, at least in part, a marine oriented technological response from this nation. In short, we need desperately a national marine policy which takes into consideration these new realities. It must not,

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
I say, Sir, be a regional or a parochial policy. International trade and resource development are national issues-national pocketbook issues, I might say.
Now, the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association reports that in December of last year employment reached a ten-year low of 8,500 people, a drop of some 5,700 people or 40 per cent of their work force. In one area alone, namely the Atlantic trawler fleet, there is a need for ship replacement over the next ten years which will mean over $3 billion worth of shipbuilding work. Much of this will be lost to Canadian industry unless there is a change in the present policy which encourages domestic fishing operators to buy offshore. Not a single fishing vessel was ordered from Canadian yards in 1982. However, five were imported for a total of 27 trawlers brought in since 1979.
Our ability, Sir, to compete in world markets, our ability to control and protect our resources, impinges directly on the economic well-being of the nation as a whole. National marine policies which touch on such issues are as important to the people of Alberta or the people of Saskatchewan as they are to the people of Shelburne, Nova Scotia, or Liverpool, or Bridgewater or Lunenburg or Halifax. I say, Sir, that the national interest must come first. We must not confuse, for example, the laudable desire to build ships in Canada or create a fleet carrying the Canadian flag with the need first to get our goods to market in the most cost effective and efficient manner possible.
The objective in shipping, and I speak here with some experience, is to move cargo and not just to sail ships. The creation of a Canadian technology that would help support and control northern and offshore resource development presumes by definition the manufacture of made at home solutions to our problems. Perhaps what we should do in this area, in the short term at least, is to make it financially attractive for Canadians who now own vessels flying foreign flags to register those ships at home.
A national marine policy must be pragmatic, flexible and designed to encourage a range of responses to what I perceive is a wide range of challenges. There is no doubt in my mind that we are equal to the task of creating a policy which constitutes an optimum response to the marine problems which, I submit, now confront us.
I realize that the creation of such a policy will require that the task become something more of a national interest than I perceive it to be at present. But the fact that the time we have in which to act on these problems is rapidly growing short may provide the necessary sense of urgency.
Meanwhile, I am personally comforted by the fact that twice before in its history, this country that we all love so well, this Canada of ours, has been a major seafaring power and, in
my opinion, there is absolutely no reason why we cannot become one for the third time.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise and speak on Bill C-151, an Act to provide supplementary borrowing authority. However, I find it irresponsible that the Government finds it necessary, after the introduction of a budget, to ask for a $4 billion padding to an already out of control deficit.
This particular Bill is one in a long line of borrowing Bills. In this session of Parliament we have witnessed Bills C-30, C-59, C-111, C-125, C-128, C-143, and now we have Bill C-151.
In its April budget, the Government had the opportunity to indicate its fiscal requirements. Now it has chosen to seek more money after the fact, for some purpose it will not reveal to Parliament, a cushion of $2 billion for this year and a $2 billion pork barrel for the future.
One thing is certain with this Government, for every $3 that it spends it must borrow $1. Government Members state that one must borrow to stimulate. There is no stimulation in this borrowing, only regression.
In an atmosphere of mistrust, one must examine where some of the funds now being requested will go. It is clear from the Government's action that the employment situation and the future employment prospects will remain dismal for at least two million unemployed in this country for at least the next foreseeable few years. At precisely a time when recovery should be encouraged, a series of regressive tax measures are scheduled to pay for the enormous deficit that this Goverment has inflicted on Canadians. We will spend the first 18 months of economic recovery going back to square one.
One of the principal aspects of the Goverment's special recovery program is the so-called Special Recovery Projects of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) which are to be funded at $2.2 billion over the next four years. Only $1.5 billion of this represents new spending, of which $460 million is expected to be spent in the 1983-84 fiscal year. No project in this program can be under way until at least October of 1983. The impact upon the unemployed in Canada will therefore be delayed at least that long.
Unlike most Canadians, the Liberals do not understand that they have to pay as they go. Heavy borrowing and Government projections place a majority of tax increases in place for sometime after the next federal election. It is a deliberate attempt to stifle an incoming Government and to reduce the range of options it will be able to undertake to put this country back on the road to recovery. Instead of real job creation and deficit control, the Government is increasing net future tax increases totalling $5.7 billion over the next four years and deficits totalling more than $102 billion between now and 1986.
May 10, 1983

In their analysis of the Government's economic position, economists say that it will "have a negative impact on consumer spending by next year, reducing chances for the strong consumer-led recovery the Government is counting on".
On a fiscal year basis, the new tax measures give consumers a $75 million gain this year but take back $365 million and $1.3 billion respectively in the following three years. Canadians needed an across the board decrease in federal sales tax or a shifting forward of next year's anticipated income tax refunds to aid consumers and help the recovery through consumer spending.
The Government has repeatedly demonstrated that it is incompetent, untrustworthy and bankrupt of ideas to effectively govern this nation. It has undermined confidence in the future of Canada and broken down the spirit of co-operation and entrepreneurship that has built this country. The Government has betrayed historic liberalism in favour of a Government-dominated and socialistic controlled society, giving themselves the right to intervene in every facet of society.
The Government has misled Canadians on oil prices, interest rates, job creation, megaprojects, property rights and tax reform, only to mention a few. This so-called Liberal Party has been in power so long that it has lost touch with democracy while muzzling Parliament, changing the law through regulations and Orders in Council and hiding behind Crown corporations and partisan faceless bureaucrats.
The Government's record speaks for itself. There are over two million unemployed and investment has been driven out of the country. Over $10 billion left the country in 1981 because Canadians moved their money to a more receptive investment climate. This money could have created at least 400,000 new jobs in the private sector.
Economic performance in Canada has been dismal. Canada's over-all economic performance now ranks fortieth behind such countries as Equador, Taiwan, Burma, Cyprus, Panama and Algeria. The OECD ranks Canada twenty-fourth and last among all the major industrialized nations in the world. What is the Liberal answer to this? It appoints Donald Macdonald at $800 to $900 per day plus expenses to produce a report at least two years after his appointment.
In November, 1981, the then Minister of Finance predicted an $11 billion deficit. It is now over $30 billion and climbing. The Auditor General says that major Government Departments are sloppy money managers, that there is no direction in personnel management, that 70 per cent of Government contracts are issued without tender, and that there is little or no accountability for millions of dollars poured into Crown corporations.
It would be fair to assume that what is expected of the taxpayer of Canada in the realm of accountability should also be expected of those who govern, particularly at the federal Cabinet level. But of course this is not the case as this Bill C-151 and the previous borrowing Bill C-143 indicate.
.Bill C-143 was the largest borrowing Bill, for $19 billion, in the history of Canada. Only a month later we are asked for an additional $14.7 billion in borrowing authority. Of that, $4
Borrowing Authority
billion will be used, without doubt, to buy votes and pork barrel just before the next election.
Accountability is the cornerstone of the fiscal system of this country. The standard of accountability expected of those who deal with the disposition of taxes raised is far less onerous and in fact downright sloppy. The annual Report of the Auditor General of Canada is replete with page after page of instances in which the Auditor General is not permitted to delve into the affairs of federal Government Crown corporations.
According to the Auditor General, accountability has been limited, particularly as far as Parliament is concerned. Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of Government activities. The growing practice of using Crown corporations to conduct a widening range of Government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibilities for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds. The existing legislative framework for creating, monitoring and, where necessary, changing this abuse should be addressed by the House.
Nothing is being done to address waste such as has been reported by the Auditor General. Inadequate management controls in overpayments totalling $285.3 million have occurred under four major energy programs by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Department of Public Works failed to recover expenditures from Canada Post Corporation of $61 million. During fiscal 1981 the Unemployment Insurance Commission is estimated to have paid out overpayments of $178 million, and the list goes on page after page.
The accountability for public funds borrowed or otherwise has tended to decrease, and the degree of parliamentary scrutiny to which Crown Corporations are subjected varies from sporadic to virtually none. The information Parliament gets from the political appointments to these Crown Corporations with respect to activities of Crown Corporations is in most cases totally unsatisfactory. A clear authority and mandate for spending borrowed money, especially if it goes to Crown Corporations, should be spelled out and accountability to Parliament made mandatory.
The recent federal budget has a critical flaw in that it has been made to appear as offering something to everyone, but in point of fact it mortgages our future without any real current gain in consumer spending. Consumer demand is a key element in any recovery. The latest budget of the federal Government raises personal income taxes by a further $3.6 billion while at the same time increasing our national debt.
Unlike Prime Minister Thatcher or President Reagan, our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) intends to cut the deficit by increasing spending as well as taxes. The share of Gross National Product now taken by Governments in Canada has already hit 40 per cent and is still rising.
We cannot afford to throw money around at a time when every third dollar spent is not covered by revenue but has to be

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
borrowed. You cannot increase investment unless consumption accelerates. If this does not happen, consumer demand will likely stagnate, which will be coupled with increased taxes along with high profile public works programs.
The only light at the end of the tunnel in this country is the fact that the international economy shows signs of improvement. If we had a Government which could complement this recovery with positive private sector confidence in this country we would indeed see a significant turnaround in the near future. Every time the Government borrows large amounts of money, the private sector must meet Government sector financing head on. The result is increased pressure on inflation and higher interest rates.
Bill C-151 and all the other borrowing Bills for which this Government has come to Parliament this session is an exercise in fiscal insolvency. Based on the financial requirements of $26.7 billion and existing borrowing authority of $16 billion, Bill C-151 should be requesting from Parliament $10.7 billion, not $14.7 billion.
The $2 billion cushion for this year is horrendous. However, the second $2 billion that is being requested from the people of Canada as a debt for their children and their children's children can exist indefinitely. I believe it is a conscious effort on the part of the Government to deal with figures of such magnitude as to dwarf the ability of the average Canadian to understand the financial ruin of his or her country.
Is this Bill, one in a steady stream, one that Canadians are to expect as this Government buys time as well as tries to buy votes as it grasps for power?
The extra funds that are being requested in Bill C-151 do not respect any attempt to live within one's means. This should be particularly true for a Government if any example is to be made. The slush funds that this Government keeps to pay off the Donald Macdonalds and the Alistair Gillespies of this country must stop.
The change that is coming will benefit all Canadians. I hope it comes before this current gang makes a bigger mess out of our economy and our country than it has already created.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions, or comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart).

Madam Speaker, I stand once again to register my deep disgust with this Government over its fiscal ineptitude, its horrendous mismanagement of funds and especially its flagrant disdain of the serious and growing debt it is imposing on the nation. Trusting this Government financially is like sending Jesse James to the bank with your bank deposit. For the seventh time in this session of Parliament, the longest session in history and still to be concluded, this Government is coming to seek permission to borrow more money. It approaches this House only three weeks after bringing in a budget which added $31 billion to our existing gross national debt of a staggering $134 billion.
With this Bill it wants to increase that burden by an additional $14.7 billion. Of this amount, $2 billion does not have to
be used this year; it may be carried forward into the future. The Government thus has a cushion of $2 billion for this year plus another cushion of $2 billion to be used in any year. Maybe it will be used for advertising. The federal Government is now the largest advertiser in the land, and perhaps the money will be used for the next election campaign to tell Canadians how good the Liberal Government has been.
I do not think any Canadian really wants to trust this Government with any more money than is necessary. Approval of this Bill would bring our gross national debt into the $180 billion range and this figure will likely soon reach the $200 billion mark. It is a legacy of debt to our children. It is disgraceful and it is disastrous for the country.
The projected financial requirements of this Government for the next four fiscal years total $93 billion. There is every reason to assume that the Government will be repeatedly back before the House over the next few years asking for permission to borrow even more money. Canadians' only hope in all this is that a general federal election will be called soon so that this Government can be turfed out and an end put to this greedy and irresponsible grab of taxpayers' dollars.
The debt created by this Government and being added to by this Government is becoming, if it has not already become, a permanent fixture in our lives. Not a very pleasant reality, I am sure.
A noted economist was reported as saying that even an economy with full employment could not wipe out Canada's debt load. Imagine that even with full employment! It is unreasonable to assume that the deficit we now bear is cyclical and will vanish when things get better. This is just not the case. Yet when introducing his budget last month, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) had the gall to claim that adding to our over-all debt would eventually reduce it. 1 do not know how he does his mathematics. Does he really think Canadians are that stupid or that gullible? The only thing I feel sad about is that not more of a clamour is being put up by the Canadian public.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is the great man who gave us the just society. Now we have just a society. He gave us "the land is strong". We know the land is strong otherwise we would not have been able to stagger under the burden that we have had. It is the Government that is weak. The same Prime Minister who years ago boasted he had wrestled inflation to the ground now has a Finance Minister who claims he can beat the deficit into submission. That is tough talk, but that is all it is, talk. Talking will not eliminate the deficit, and that must be done before this country can prosper. Increasing the tax burden on Canadians will not eliminate the deficit. Further spending will not eliminate it. Only a cut in spending and proper fiscal management will do so, coupled with immediate action to halt unnecessary spending. That will put the brakes on the runaway deficit and it will allow the Government to gain control of the situation, if it is willing to bring in the measures to do it. A prime measure, indeed an absolute
May 10, 1983

must, would be the strict adherence to the historic and traditional necessity of accountability.
This Government is not spending its own money and it is not borrowing money in its own name. It is spending the money of the Canadian taxpayer and it is borrowing money which will be paid back by the Canadian taxpayer. Surely the Canadian taxpayer has the right to demand accountability from those who take these actions on their behalf.
Accountability means responsibility. We hear so much of human rights, but how many times do we hear about human responsibility and the responsibility to the Canadian people of that Cabinet across the way? When you use something that belongs to someone else, you are responsible for how it is used. When you do something in someone else's name, you have the responsibility to do it right. If you fail on one or both counts you must consider yourself responsible. You must consider yourself accountable. It is very simple, it is traditional, it is honourable and it is a concept that should be followed in this House, but which heretofore has not been. It is a concept of which the Government is either unaware or absolutely dismisses. This lack of accountability on the part of Government takes many forms. We have Ministers avoiding responsibility for their own actions and those of their Departments-such as the unresigned, the unrepentent leaker across the way. We have Ministers who avoid the responsibility of Parliament by announcing Government policy in public forums, such as the letter of the Prime Minister in the press today and his three stilted television appearances. We have Ministers who either participate in or condone the questionable dealings of former colleagues vis-a-vis Gillespie. We have a Government which avoids its responsibility to Parliament and to Canadians by an abusive use of Orders in Council to create everything from Crown corporations to positions of patronage, to odious and objectionable legislation, and even to internment camps. This deliberate avoidance of accountability is costly to Canadian taxpayers as well as being an affront to Parliament, to ourselves who represent the people and to the people themselves.
Many strong and reasoned objections have been raised regarding the Government's seemingly endless creation of Crown corporations. In his recent Report the Auditor General raised the alarm regarding the dangers inherent and evident in the existence of these agencies of Government. He said-and rightly so-that Crown corporations are "sub-Government" and that they should and must be accountable to Parliament and to the shareholders, which of course is the Canadian public.
It is common knowledge that the nation's actual deficit is far higher than the figures I have just stated. The debts being incurred by Crown corporations are not included in the Government total and they are not audited. In many instances tax dollars are being poured into these corporations with scant regard for the manner in which the funds are being spent. The actions of management are not subject to public or parliamentary scrutiny, and only inadvertently do we learn of the magnitude of the waste involved or of the gross ineptness of operations. I refer, for example, to CIDA and its top-heavy
Borrowing Authority
management, the debt load of Haiti of $22 million of taxpayers' money and the project being scrapped. There is no accountability and there have been fraudulent payments specifically pinpointed as being fraudulent, such as one for over $100,000. No one is accountable, and there have been no firings.
The Government's handling of the Crown-owned aircraft company, Canadair, is the most recent example of the inefficiency and waste of Government intervention and why it needs to borrow more money. The Government, without consulting Parliament, has given the company more than $1.5 billion, and the Prime Minister has said that Canadair will likely be asking for more money later this year. The final bill to the taxpayer for the development of the Challenger executive jet may reach the staggering sum of $2.3 billion, for an aircraft fitted with Lycoming helicopter engines.
Adding to the problem, the Government recently put Canadair under the management and control of yet another Crown corporation-the Canada Development Investment Corporation. It sounds wonderful! CDIC is not accountable to Parliament, so there can be little public confidence in entrusting this Corporation to handle the problems of another. The very creation of CDIC and the manner in which it is being run gives clear indication to any Canadian willing to think about it of the fundamental and costly error Government makes when it enters the private marketplace. Formed initially to get the Government out of the Canada Development Corporation, over which it tried to but could not gain control, CDIC was handed responsibility for Ottawa's interest in half a dozen firms. Naturally the corporation exists by virtue of 17 Orders in Council, not by the authority of Parliament. Sell it and reduce the deficit; that is what really counts, not borrowing money.
There has been debate over whether the Corporation was created to permit Government to gain control and power over the private sector or to provide more positions of patronage. It is my feeling that both motives apply. The chairman of CDIC is none other than Maurice Strong, a long-time Liberal and friend of the Prime Minister. The company president is Joel Bell, the architect of the Government's short-lived competitions policy, of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, that millstone around our necks, and the national energy policy. Lots of luck at the gas pumps! Joel Bell was also the man who devised the formula for a tax on consumers to pay for Petro-Canada's purchase of Petrofina. That tax is continuing even though it has been paid. This year Canadians will probably pay $800 million at the pumps, which they should not be paying, to bail out Dome Petroleum. The two men running the Corporation report to Senator Jacob Austin, formally the Prime Minister's principal secretary and directly connected with Canada's involvement in the uranium cartel-another sweetheart! All three of them are dedicated interventionists. Given what we have seen from their past accomplishments, we can be sure their attitudes have not changed.

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
In addition to Canadair, another Crown corporation now under the umbrella of CDIC is the de Havilland Aircraft company. It too is financially strapped and has been offered a pledge of financial support using Canadian tax dollars. Just this week the Government announced that it will be purchasing a number of Dash-7 aircraft produced by de Havilland for use as water bombers. Of course there is the budget scam known as a job-creation program for the purchase of water bombers, but it all depends upon whether the Province matches the federal Government. It seems that the only reliable customer for this Crown corporation is the Crown itself.
Earlier the Canadian military purchased a few of the Dash-7s for use as executive transport in Europe. The planes were purchased by the Department of National Defence as a replacement for the Cosmopolitan aircraft. The age of the plane to be replaced necessitated a new model, but the underlying reason for the purchase of the Dash-7s was that Canada wanted to sell them to overseas nations and we had to be seen as supporting our own product. Now we know that the $12 million Dash-7 is to be converted, to the tune of $37 million, supposedly to monitor ice. Ice could be monitored a lot cheaper than by spending $37 million on a $12 million aircraft. Canadair and de Havilland are two sinkholes now owned by Canadians who are expected to pump even more money into the gaping maws of each. As I have mentioned, the three men who now control the direction of CDIC played a large role in the creation of Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada is another perfect example of the serious problems which result when the Government intervenes in the private sector, problems which ultimately translate into debt.
Last year the Government imposed a tax upon the consumption of oil and natural gas to finance the purchase of Petrofina by Petro-Canada. As I stated, it should be over at the pumps, but Canadians are still paying that tax. Now it has decided to extend that tax to give the Crown corporation revenue to finance projects in the energy field. Grandly advertising itself as a genuine Canadian feat the corporation tells Canadians, "It's ours". According to a recent Gallup poll, Canadians do not share or accept the proud claim of possession. Some 60 per cent of those polled said they made absolutely no effort to buy their gasoline from Petro-Canada stations, and 45 per cent thought the corporation should be sold, so do I. Canadians fully realize the only thing that is ours is the debt being incurred by Petro-Canada.
Tax dollars are being used by an arm of this Crown corporation-it is a new one, another goody called Petro-Canada International-to assist developing nations to find their own sources of oil and gas. Last year the budget for Petro-Canada International was $21 million. That amount is to more than double this year to $55 million, and the person in control of it answers only to the Minister, not to the House.
Canada will spend almost $80 million in two years to help nations like Tanzania, Senegal, Thailand and Sri Lanka supposedly to become energy self-sufficient, with no assurance of achieving that. Because Petro-Canada is a Crown corporation, not accountable to Parliament or to the taxpayer, the
Government does not have to bother justifying anything. How can the Government justify taking tax money from Canadians to aid others when Canada itself is nowhere near self-sufficient in energy? The megaprojects are all cancelled, and the Beaufort Sea project is gone. It cannot even justify the millions and billions it spends on other foreign aid in the form of what it terms soft loans. The Auditor General also raised this issue at the time he presented his very interesting Report. He said that the $4 billion in interest free loans given to developing nations should really be classified as gifts and should be recognized as such for purposes of accounting. Is it any wonder we have to borrow even more billions of dollars? They have been frittered away. By keeping these gifts or grants on the books as loans, the Government is concealing funds which should properly be listed as debts.
I think it is significant that whatever area of Government we examine-and it does not matter where one looks, be it the Report of the Auditor General or the financial situation of the country-the common denominator is not deficit, it is debt. It is deep, dark, dirty, dreaded debt. We have official debts. We have Crown corporation debts. We have debts disguised as loans and letters of comfort. I would suggest that the Government write a letter of comfort to the Canadians who are underwriting these debts. The greatest comfort Canadians could have would be to receive a letter from the Government in the form of a writ announcing the calling of a federal general election. That would truly be a letter of comfort to Canadians.
The Government is before us asking for permission to plunge the nation even deeper into debt. The deficit being incurred by the Government in the name of all Canadians clearly reveals its incompetence to handle its affairs. A major part of the problem is that the Government, through Crown corporations, either establishes companies in competition with those in the private marketplace or tries desperately to salvage companies which cannot compete successfully in the marketplace.
I would now like to touch on the bilingual program in Canada. All of us support the Official Languages Act, but it is being twisted, warped and no longer has merit in the marketplace or in Government offices. Linguistics now take preference over merit. The total cost of the bilingual program, which is absolutely non-productive spending, in 1981-82 was $433,597,000. The projected cost for 1982-83 is $453,222,000.
Maybe we could take a minute to see if this is being done equitably and fairly and whether the money is being well spent. Maybe we should examine a speech by the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) to the Federation Acadienne de la Nouvelle-Ecosse on November 13, 1982. At page 2 he said:
-because everything we undertake and everything we are doing to make Canada a French state is part of a venture I have shared for many years-
On the same page he states:
-making Canada a French country both inside and outside Quebec-
May 10, 1983

If we look at the spending he is talking about, this half a billion dollars. We find that he said this at page 3:
-financial support will be required to fund the cases, to fund the actions that will force the courts to rule on what "where numbers warrant" means and what an educational institution is, because, you know you and I have a long memory now.
A little later on he states this with regard to financing:
Francophone rights cannot be bought, sold, subtracted, divided or multiplied in terms of dollars and cents in the budgets of a troubled economy, and that will apply, I promise you, for as long as I am Secretary of State for Canada. If I have to cut back some programs-and I've already done so-there is one area in which I have no intention of using the scissors: the advancement of Francophone rights in Canada.
On page 8 we read this:
Accordingly, the first thing I did when I joined the Secretary of State Department was to tell the bureaucrats to prepare a development program for French universities, or rather French universities across Canada, in light of the resources and economic characteristics of each region.
Obviously we are going to spend more money. I now refer to Hansard for March 2, 1981 page 7773 where the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) asked Question No. 1,934 as follows:
What is the budget for the current fiscal year of the Official Language Minority Groups Directorate of the Department of the Secretary of State and what is the (a) percentage (b) per capita allocation of this sum to each official language group?
The answer was:
The budget of the Official Language Minority Groups Directorate for fiscal year 1980-81 is $15 million.
The answer stated that the allocation of the budget was as follows: Francophones outside Quebec, $14,073,800 or 94 per cent, Anglophones in Quebec, $926,200 or 6 per cent. I do not call that fair. We all want and have rights in this country. That does not smack of rights to me.
The Financial Post is now carrying stories about what is happening in this country. You must be bilingual to have a job at the Fredericton airport. This applies even to those who have worked there for 15 years. I quote from the article:
None of the eight women who staff car-rental booths at the airport speaks French. To satisfy the new policy, all must either learn, or be replaced.
"1 think it's stupid" says an angry Judy Martinson.
She claims that in 12 years staffing the airport's Avis booth, she has never had problems with a customer because of language.
This is to be implemented at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, Wabush, Newfoundland, Timmins, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury and North Bay in Ontario. There will be a tremendous backlash if we do not start treating Canadians all equally.
I pointed out in the House today that $454,000, almost half a million dollars, is being allocated to the celebration of Jacques Cartier's discovery of North America. We all laud that. We applaud it. We want to do that. The total cost is $1.6 million. But when we are talking about Gilbert, the first colonizer of Newfoundland, this year we can only come up with some $394,000. Does that smack of equal rights and is the money being spent properly? There is a litany of horror
Borrowing Authority
here that does not support the merit system, only by merit of linguistics.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) in a recent speech decried the fact that he voted for this legislation. He too, as are all of us, is not opposed to the Official Languages Act, but terribly opposed to the way it is being negated. At the conclusion of his speech he said:
I must, Mr. Speaker, say to this House, to my constituents and to Canadians, that I have been betrayed in the bilingual program. I supported it. I have to ask that it revert to what it was. Canadians have been betrayed and their resources mismanaged.
That is one aspect of this. We know economically that everything smacks of mismanagement. I conclude by saying that as English-speaking Canadians, we demand fair treatment-not special treatment, just fair. We demand that the merit system remain in place. We demand that the deficit be cut and that linguistics not be given preference in the job market.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 21 I, as the Member of Parliament for Vancouver East,

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
sponsored a community meeting on unemployment which may be of considerable interest to the Members of the House and certainly, I hope, to the Government. About 150 people turned out. There was quite a mixture of unemployed people, people from different ethnic groups in my riding, representatives of Canada Employment and a number of resource persons. We were pleased that Bishop De Roo of Victoria, who is involved in the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops and their statement on "Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis", opened this session.
There was very profound discussion. Also, we had six workshops, I would like to state some of the findings of these workshops which were made up of ordinary people. People who are unemployed and very depressed came up with some very positive suggestions from which we may all learn. Also, in the householder, which was mailed to every constituent, we included a questionnaire. Replies are beginning to flood back.
I will be glad to make this available if anyone is interested. The replies to some of these questionnaires show feelings that we never see in Parliament. We have statistics, generalizations and reports. We think we know our own riding, but it really hits you when you hear from individual people. For example, an unemployed copywriter feels isolated, depressed, rejected and worthless even though he has considerable skill.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I certainly will relate it. I assumed it was implied in the topic. Much of the money to be borrowed under Bill C-151, $14 billion, will be used for job-creation programs. I wish a lot more of it was being so used. The unemployment situation in Canada is truly disastrous.
I want to go back to those very interesting recommendations which I hope will be of interest to the Government because they deal with that very thing and show how the money could be used much more effectively. Some of the human resources that do not cost much are being wasted. They could be mobilized for more self-help and positive programs.
I will mention some examples of people caught in this situation, just to bring matters down to earth. Most of us cannot even comprehend $14 billion, but my examples show real life.
There was an apartment manager and former landscaper who is now on welfare. They only help he feels he is getting from the employment office is that he has been put on a waiting list there. An unemployed secretary is losing confidence but has all kinds of good suggestions for things that could be done. A young man of Chinese extraction, aged 22 is an accountant. He has a part-time job now, after looking for a job for eight months and wasting 200 resumes in the process. A child-care worker with a university education cannot get work. There is a yardsman where crews have been reduced and he feels that the unions have not cared enough. An unemployed timekeeper with lots of experience is on welfare. A
trucker aged 53 has lost his recall rights through the union but he has ideas on employment of younger people. A single mechanic aged 25 lives in a dump and says he has lost his goals, and that to survive he begs, borrows or steals. An immigrant whose son is not working feels that we need more manufacturing and better co-operation between labour and management.
I could go on and on giving examples but there is not enough time, Mr. Speaker. I wanted to bring to the attention of the House something that is related to a Bill and the kinds of things that the money should be spent on.
In Vancouver East, unemployment has increased 125 per cent over the past year. Workers who had expectations of a good life for themselves and their families actually suffer culture shock. I find that it is almost worse for people who have been comfortable with savings and a home and who are not the chronic unemployed on welfare. They experience culture shock as they lose cars and homes and in many cases families as a direct result of unemployment. Young people told me that they cannot get into the system. They are told in grandiose terms that they are the hope of the future, the pride of tomorrow, yet they feel hopeless, disenfranchised and discouraged. They cannot get training or jobs and so cannot gain experience. Older people face extreme pressures as children in their twenties and thirties return home to become dependent on their parents.
We held this meeting in the Native Indian centre. Native people, with 75 per cent unemployment, suffer the greatest hardship. Immigrants find that their skills are not being used they cannot get welfare because they are immigrants. Often their sponsors are unemployed as well. Families are under considerable stress and are breaking up. Poverty is worse than ever and crime is increasing. This is what we were told by people working with the unemployed and by the victims of unemployment. As I said, the group came up with a number of recommendations in six workshops. They had some survival tips.
First of all, they want more information regarding Canada employment job-creation programs. The respondents to the questionnaire said over and over again that they do not know what Government programs are available.
Job-creation programs should not be restricted to those on Unemployment Insurance. This is discriminatory. Many young people and women who have not been able to get into the work force and on Unemployment Insurance feel that the jobs are going to the lucky ones, those who at least have Unemployment Insurance benefits. Welfare rates should be increased considerably. There were a number of recommendations that will be passed on to the provincial Governments. There should be free bus passes so that unemployed persons can go to look for work or training.
It was felt that much could be done in community job creation. The money that is available at present for many short-term, stop-gap job-creation programs might be better
May 10, 1983

used in co-operation with the community to create community enterprises that would offer more permanent jobs. That would be a better investment for some of this $14 billion in the Bill. Government grants and programs should respond more to the people. Again, the bureaucrats and the Government lay this on from Ottawa and take a long time to set it up, so much money is spent on the bureaucracy when there could be a more creative way of working with the communities and using their ideas. Action is needed to minimize bureaucratic red tape and to improve Government services. It was felt that we should reexamine the whole question of obsolescence and expand training programs.
There were a lot of complaints about training programs, Mr. Speaker. The Minister says that the new Training Act will be beneficial and more programs will be available. But people in the community find that there is a five-year wait for many training programs.
The Government should introduce long-term employment programs instead of band-aid programs. There should be more offices for part-time and casual employers. In Vancouver there is one office that is quite separate and is inaccessible to a lot of people. It was suggested that there offices should be part of every employment office so that more part-time and casual jobs would be readily available.
There should be job creation for native people who face the greatest unemployment, and this should be given higher priority bu all levels of Government. There should also be affirmative action. There should be more funds available for reforestation jobs and there should be an increase in the amount of Government land available for public housing programs. More environmental cleanup and pollution control in the rivers and lakes as well as the other areas is required. Native counsellors are needed to replace non-natives to work with native people in employment offices.
The workshop on technological change and training had some very good suggestions. It felt there must be more education of the public about technological change. There is great fear and misconception abroad. This requires long-term planning toward human beings. I should like to stress that, Mr. Speaker. We are talking about incentives for high-tech training, and a lot of the money provided by the Bill will likely go toward tech-change incentives. Yet we are not planning for human beings. We cannot stop technological change; we need it but we can also invest in human beings and retraining for alternate kinds of jobs, for shorter work hours. More attention should be paid to a guaranteed income.
People should begin to prepare for several career changes throughout their lives. Education programs must be changed. It was pointed out repeatedly that our institutions are out of date and are not really training people for the future. A fundamental restructuring of education is needed. High school students are being misinformed. They are being offered training programs in traditional careers which are no longer relevant.
Employed and unemployed people must work co-operatively. Unions must be just as concerned with the unemployed as they
Borrowing Authority
are with union members and people who have never been in a union.
The Unemployment Insurance Act should be changed. It is based on the assumption that people are cheaters. There is a negative, punitive quality in our Unemployment Insurance Act. Applications for Unemployment Insurance should be simplified.
Wages for Government programs are too low. There should be a minimum wage standard and better co-operation between federal and provincial Governments to make sure that we do not exploit people who are victims of unemployment.
We had assumed that the youth would go into other workshop groups, but they said we have forgotten them and left them out just as everyone else does. Of course, a group was formed especially for them. They felt that unemployed youth and students should not be treated differently in the Summer Canada Program, for example, which excludes youth who are not students, that this was a kind of elitist approach. Young people who have been out of school and out on the streets all winter still cannot get summer jobs. Therefore, they felt there should be general job-creation programs to open up opportunities for all youth. Youth should have a voice. There should be an advisory committee of youth, and youth must organize and lobby and be heard. Out of this meeting, I am glad to see that they agreed to form such a group.
Private industry should do more to help young people to get jobs and experience, even those who are training in colleges. The co-operative kind of training which is being done in some colleges, where there is training on the job, is extremely important.
