Mr. Speaker, I am going to spend the 20 minutes at my disposal by taking advantage of this opportunity to tell the House some of the horrendous nightmare stories which have occurred because we have an uncaring Government which refuses to take into consideration the wishes of the majority of its constituents on priority matters pertaining to the spending of our dollars. I am going to deal particularly with the subject of the Metric Commission. The Metric Commission to some Hon. Members in the House might be perceived to be the kind of commission which is doing a service for the Canadian people. In reality what it is doing is creating one of the greatest cost drains to the consumers in Canada. At the same time it is causing the Government of Canada to require huge sums of money-and I am not talking about thousands or millions but about billions of dollars- which are being consumed by the Government of Canada, through the suggestions of the Metric Commission, to bring about this forced "march to metric".
It would not be so bad, Mr. Speaker, if we had a Government which would instruct, request or demand of our Metric Commission that it show some cost justification for a forced "march to metric". What we have is a situation where we have to go south of the border to the United States in order to obtain a study which was taken there so we would have some idea of just what it is costing to ge metric in Canada. I can report to this House that in the United States, the General Accounting Office of the United States Government commissioned a study to find out what it would cost if the American people went metric against their will. The final conclusions of the GAO are that the major reasons why the American industry and businesses backed away from going metric is that it would cost between $60 billion and $100 billion. This is what it would cost in the United States if it were to bring about a mandatory "march to metric".
In Canada there was also a report, and an update, on the move to metric during the short time of the Conservative Government in 1979. The big stumbling block concerning metrication in the U.S. was the inability to determine costs and benefits which were cost justified. A report prepared by the Conservative Government in 1979 stated that, based on the limited cost data available to the Comptroller General of Canada, the cost would be somewhere around $100 billion in the United States. So we not only have it confirmed by the General Accounting Office in the United States, but it is reported in our own records in the House of Commons.
Having said that, I wonder what is the reason that we have such an interested group of metric commissioners spending at will hundreds of millions of dollars to bring about this "march to metric". After four years I finally obtained a list of the metric commissioners; where they came from, what they did, how much they get and why they are there. We have a litany of Liberal involvement in Party politics sitting as 20 paid commissioners on the Metric Commission. What do these 20 commissioners receive in remuneration for their work on the Metric Commission, which is paid for by borrowed tax dollars by this Canadian Government? They receive $250 a day plus all their expenses. We have Liberal campaign managers. We have Liberal fund raisers. We have Liberal candidates to feed
it in provincial elections. Not all of these people, but most of them, constitute active Liberal involvement in Liberal activities across this nation.
We are to believe, as Members of Parliament, that we are going metric because industry wants it, because the construction industry wants it, the industrial sector wants it and the grocers want it. That is simply not true, Mr. Speaker, and I say this with all due respect to those who are in the House of Commons. The grocers did not want it. They passed a resolution at their meeting before the Order in Council was passed that they did not wish to spend the money on going metric in the retail food sector of Canada. The Government could have saved $32 million a year if it had listened to the retail sector, particularly the grocery sector, who specifically held press conferences and attended meetings of Government officials and said it did not wish to go metric.
What about the people? What do the people think about a $32 million Metric Commission budget? That is $3 million in salaries, $2 million in propaganda, advertising. What do the people of Canada think? We could refer to surveys carried out by independent groups. We could go to Dominion Store which surveyed not less than 68 per cent of its store retail purchasers who did not wish to go metric. We could go to the Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers, 85 per cent of whom were surveyed. We could go to CKO, National News, Radio which commissioned an independent consultant in Toronto to carry out a survey. What was the result of that? Even the school children, even the young people in the age group of 18 to 25 do not wish to go metric. And we have a Metric Commission laced with dollars by this Government, this uncaring Government. We have a Metric Commission laced with taxpayers' dollars which is spending hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
We thought in 1974, when we set up this Metric Commission at an annual budget of $44,000, that that would be ample in order to assist the various sectors in this country to go metric. That $44,000 annual budget in 1973-74 has grown to a $32 million annual budget with a $3,200,000 annual payroll for the Metric Commission in its ivory tower here in Ottawa. We saw an Order in Council passed by the Liberal Government in 1971 which said there shall be up to 15 commissioners, people with their snouts in the trough, the pork barrel group of Liberal workers, at a daily rate of $250 plus expenses. Orders in Council have since been passed requiring more metric commissioners; there are over 20 of them now. Why, they have the editor emeritus of the Lethbridge Herald, a Liberal, whose job it is to shadow me across the country writing letters to the editor. This same Cleo Mowers, metric commissioner, editor emeritus of the Lethbridge Herald, while a commissioner, was paid by the Toronto Globe and Mail to write an article on the editorial page of the Globe and Mail on the reasons why we should go metric.

I admire very much the crusade he is carrying in Canada against the mandatory imposition of the metric measurement system. He is to be commended, and he certainly has the support of his colleagues, at least on this side of the House.
We are dealing with yet another borrowing Bill, Bill C-151. The Government is back once more to the House asking for another $14.7 billion, at least $4 billion of which is not really needed. It is not in the Government spending plans or its budget, and the Government cannot justify it in this further request for taxpayers' money.
Of the $4 billion that is surplus in this seventh request to this session of Parliament, $2 billion is a little cushion, a little pad, $2 billion which the Government wants to tuck under the
Borrowing Authority
mattress to carry over into the next fiscal year beginning April 1, 1984.
What we have seen in the budget is a program of immediate spending with the idea of assisting some consumer spending, the idea of giving a lift to the spending and the cash flow of the country whereby the Government can say its policies and its six and five program and all of these things are working. We hear time and time again from one Minister after the other and even from some bank presidents in Canada that things are good, that we are through the recession, that we will come out of it and there are bright days ahead. With the spending programs of the recent budget, the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) assures there is a bubble. Yes, there is a bubble coming as a result of the policies in the United States. Our great market to the south has its inflation under control, its interest rates are down and normally there is in Canada a nine-month lag following corrective measures or erroneous measures that take place in the U.S.A.
As I said, we are into the seventh borrowing Bill. I might remind Hon. Members that these borrowing Bills are in addition to Section 38 of the Financial Administration Act which gives the Government automatic power to borrow to retire maturing instruments or debt already in the system. Unless you get a memorandum from the Department of Finance and understand fully what this total borrowing is in order to handle maturing debt plus the interventionist programs of this interventionist Government, we really have difficulty in keeping a handle on just what is going on.
Bill C-151 is one more example of the cry of some of us that the whole process of supply and expenditure in the Canadian Government is out of control. The whole federal system is out of control. Both the federal and provincial systems in this country are out of control as a result of this idea that all answers to all problems of the population can be solved by the Government.
It seems that we have been conditioned to expect that Government will take care of all our problems and we no longer have a sense of self reliance among ourselves as a people. We are used to so much rhetoric on recovery and on the subject matter of Government programs, what they will do here and what they will do there that year after year we get program after program. If you go back and take a good, hard look, you find they are the same old programs on which the Government has not spent money that are being recycled with new words and being brought forward with new headlines to keep the people under some kind of opiate and under the illusion that this place is doing something constructive.
We now hear from the Minister of Finance and other Ministers in this Government that the recession is over, that we have this bubble of recovery. We heard that things are going to be good. We have had notice that even things like tax-free savings for equity in a home can be used to purchase furniture and consumer goods if spent within the next immediate period of time. All of these things are stimulants, but do we see the consumer really buying these measures and this

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
rhetoric that all is well and that all will start moving again? Yes, I see out on the West Coast some recovery in housing sales. Prices have dropped about one third. Interest rates are down, and there is some stimulus and some movement there. If recovery is really on the way, Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that we will not have a sustainable recovery in this country until we start to see capital goods move and until we start to see business and organizations within our economy that add to the value of goods starting to buy new plants, new equipment and replacing equipment which can no longer add to or improve productivity. Until we start to see a solid movement in capital goods, it is my opinion that we will not see a sustainable recovery.
Most people from the business community in Canada are quite pleased with the budget. It appears that the apparent continuing intervention and the apparent continuing attack on the disposable income of Canadian business and Canadian people has been arrested with the most recent budget of this Government. The Minister of Finance has certainly arrested the great concern we had as a result of the series of three previous budgets.
If the Government really means what it says in this budget, if the Government is withdrawing its interventionist attack on the business community, and if it really wants a sustained forward adjustment in the Canadian community, we will have to stop placing the blame for our dilemma on the cold winds of economic recession that blow from the north, that blow from Europe and that blow from the United States. For many years now we in Canada have been sowing the seeds of our own cyclical economic troubles.
I can remember a couple of years ago having the privilege of being invited as a Canadian delegate to a conference in Ditchley, England on the impact of lower rates of economic growth on western nations. I was shocked to find myself taking the minority position of one at a world conference table saying that the western world had to get used to lower rates of growth if we were to adjust to the future ahead because the Third World was rising and demanding its fair share of limited world resources and limited world energy. To stimulate consumerism is okay for the short-term effect. That is what the budget is doing. But you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the budget and the spending required in Bill C-151 is short-term spending and short-term stimulation, with the cost of this immediate policy of this Government being postponed to 1985-1986.
What we are dealing with in this Parliament today is very short-term. The Government is not addressing long-term correction which will involve fundamental and basic attitudinal and anticipated change right across Canada. We hear the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) speak in these terms. He fascinates me when he speaks in these terms. But in my opinion he keeps blowing it by coming up with half truths or contradictory actions following a fundamental truth that he is addressing. As a result, he has thrown the country into confusion. He has thrown people like myself into confusion and his credibility is wanting in terms of long-term correction. His Government is involved in short-term, immediate political correction in preparation for an election down the road.
Whoever wins that election will have the job of paying for these immediate short-term policies.
Consumers are not buying. As I mentioned, there is some movement in housing on the West Coast, but basically consumers are sitting on their savings and reducing their debt. Until there is stability in the system, until we get away from the short-term cyclical interest rate, until we do some planning into the future as individuals, as corporations and as a nation, I suggest the measures in place today are very short-term indeed. Now we find banks pushing money. They are advertising and saying, "Come borrow, come buy", just after going through a couple of years of seizing, bankrupting and forcing people into soft and hard receiverships.
Every Canadian is involved in the recession. All expectations across the land, the expectations with which we have grown to live over the last two decades, have to be questioned, until we get those expectations back down to practical, realistic levels, until we start adjusting our attitudes to include a little compassion for the person who does not have a job. We have to get such persons back into the work force. We, the organized and the privileged, have to give a little and share a little in order to spread the economic adjustment we have to face over the next years. Until we get into this mode of thinking and accept the fact that our expectation levels have to come down and to be adjusted, what will we accomplish? We must get back to work and stop spending Government money. We must stop Government interventionist programs for losers and protectionism. The sooner we reduce our expectation levels and accept the fact that we have to move into a world of free trade the better. We must stop backing losers and start encouraging winners. Until we do that, the nation will not move ahead. It will not happen. All this spending effort-the budgets and the borrowing-will always be wasted until our basic anticipation levels and attitudes as a people and a nation change. That is the challenge ahead of us, and recovery will only come when this change takes place. I would personally like us to stop playing games with political rhetoric. All Parties in the House should start to address the fundamental need for change in our great country.
We can talk all we want about the magic of high technology ahead, that everything will be resolved with high-tech. If we drive our cars through Silicon Valley in California, we see that every parking lot in front of every high-tech factory is absolutely jammed with cars. If we continue to drive through the automobile assembly and manufacturing area of Oakland, we see grass growing through the blacktop parking lots and there are no cars. That is the magnitude of change which is taking place in the world.
We politicians in the House are not addressing this matter because we are too interested in short-term political gain and in short-term support of losers. It will come with change in attitude and it will come when we stop talking and dreaming about an industrial strategy which no one in the House can
May 10, 1983

define. It is just great for the socialists to yack about an industrial strategy, but the country needs an industrial environment. When we have an industrial environment which once again gets Government out of the boardrooms, off the backs of entrepreneurs, inventors and risk takers, and allows these people to activate that exciting thought and work process, we will start to move ahead.
My appeal in this debate on Bill C-151 is that the Government should keep moving back from its 15 years of growing intervention in the marketplace. Once again it should stabilize and spread the decision-making base across the country. Once again it should create an environment which attracts the brains of the world to Canada as it once did. If Canada did not have a good research and development environment in the private sector at one time, the Cowplands and the Mitchells would not be in Canada doing what they are doing for the country and for the world today in the area of high-tech. The spin-off in high-tech is unbelievable, even with what we have in the country. But it will take a change in attitude on the part of all of us, particularly on the part of politicians, if it is to come about.
I do not want to compete with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who is engaged in conversation. I can hardly hear myself as a result. Mr. Speaker, would you call for a little order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I said, the supply and expenditure process of Government is out of control. If I may, I would like to return to that and say that if we are to give credibility to the House and to the Government, as Members of Parliament we will have to address this issue. As politicians we have gone through decades of politics of competition, being big spenders and promising programs. As a result, we have created a modern monolithic Government which is really in the control of bureaucrats. It is not in the control of Government Members, although they are responsible for the continuation of it and the deliberation of policy. If we are to address this, we in the House of Commons must learn a technique with which to build a system of calling both the Government and the bureaucrats to account. We must ensure that the criteria against which programs are delivered and against which spending is made are in fact enforced and adhered to as the functions go on.
The reason I raise this is that I could not believe what was developing the other day out of an examination of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts under paragraph 15.9. This was the paragraph in which the Auditor General drew to our attention that $2.7 million of taxpayers' money had been delivered to an organization in the Province of Quebec. The money had been deposited in the Mercantile Bank and, as soon as the bank had the money three days later, it bankrupted the company.
When the tax resource has been delivered under the criterion of being of significant benefit to Canada and for the creation of permanent payrolls, when the administrators of
Borrowing Authority
programs such as that are careless enough to deliver that magnitude of assistance-and it lasts three days-when the beneficiaries are the shareholders of a company which went bankrupt because its bank indebtedness had been reduced, and when the beneficiary is a bank, I suggest it is just the tip of the iceberg in a behavioural and an accountability problem that Hon. Members on all sides of the House are not addressing. Credibility and respect for this institution will not return until we as Members of Parliament organize ourselves in a proper committee structure and until we demand the research resource we require to use the information available to us to create a method of disclosure which will eventually bring the behavioural problems in the system to account. The challenge is ours. Admittedly we are big spenders; we do not want to bring about a condition of accountability and control over the Government.
I am saying to you, Sir, and to my colleagues in this House that until we start to change our attitudes and demand of the system some credibility and accountability, this out of control spending process will continue. The system is going to collapse under it. That is why I appreciate the opportunity I have been given to offer a few comments on this seventh borrowing Bill in this session of the thirty-second Parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Are Hon. Members rising to ask questions?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you and I are beginning to be old debating partners because for the seventh time I am standing here as part of my duty to my constituents, a duty which I gladly accept and which they reinforce every time I speak to them, to oppose this outrageous borrowing Bill of the Liberal Government of Canada. This Government was elected on promises to reduce Government in people's lives, but since 1980 it has increased the role of Government dramatically. It has increased the debt being foisted on to our young people and which will affect them for the rest of their days. Indeed, it will affect our grandchildren.
There have been 15 PC Members and five NDP Members who have spoken to this Bill. From the Government side, there has been only one Minister and two Members. Are they responding to their constituents? I go into their ridings and talk to the people. They no more want to have their children and grandchildren being run into debt than the people in my riding. Obviously Liberal backbenchers are getting the same message, that this has to stop. Are they rising in this House to object? They are not. Indeed, they will once again stand and vote more deficit and debt for this nation.
Let us look at the statistics. The Government said it needed $26.7 billion in financial requirements this year. It already has $16 billion. On principle, one might say they need $10.7 billion. That should be the maximum amount of this Bill. When you look beyond that, you find it has $5 billion in the bank. That is the cash it now has. In fact, what it really needs in this borrowing Bill is $5.7 billion.

May 10, 1983
Borrowing Authority
Why is the Government coming to this House for $14.7 billion? Why are Liberal backbenchers not objecting to a Cabinet taking $14.7 billion in competition with our own people who need that money to put into plants, equipment and job creation? Creating jobs increases revenues to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It reduces the welfare rolls and Unemployment Insurance. The Government should not be competing in the marketplace for $14.7 billion, but it is.
There are several possibilities. One is that the accounts that have been put before the House are incorrect. Possibly the revenue flow into the Consolidated Revenue Fund is down dramatically. We have heard from accountants that tax forms being filled out this year do not show the same type of income tax due and payable as in years before.
I have talked to some of my constituents. Because interest rates and costs have gone up so dramatically, there is no profit left in the system. Of course, there are fewer people working now than even a few months ago Therefore, revenues are down. If the Government needs $14.7 billion because revenues will be down, why does it not share that with this House? Each of us, whether on the Government side or Opposition side, has the long-time ancient historic responsibility, which is the number one reason why we are here, to control the financial purse strings of the Crown, and now the Cabinet of some 36 kings and queens.
The other possibility is that it is simply an election slush fund. That may well be it. Another possibility is that there is a deliberate strategy to maximize the deficits. In some of the programs that have been announced recently several hundreds of millions of dollars will be spread out over several years. The Government is fixing this into law. That may well be a Liberal Party strategy to bind any future Government that may not be Liberal-it certainly will not be Liberal-to any meaningful programs.
If that is so, that is the most abominable, dastardly thing they can do. It is trying to control the people of this country beyond the grave. Within this last year it should not have put policies in place that will go four or five years into the future, binding the then Government.
Some people have suggested it may be part of the continuing strategy to impoverish segments of our society so that they are controlled by Government. At one time our senior citizens had a lot of freedom. They worked, put a little money aside and had a nest-egg for their retirement. They were free. They did not need the old age pension. The Old Age Security was nice, but they were free to do other things.
When a Government has these deficits, rates of inflation and high interest rates, it leads to a collapse. Inflation destroys the nest-egg of these retired people. Members are getting more and more people coming into their offices who feel that they are just a ward of the Government, that without their Old Age Security cheque, they could not buy groceries. Are these
people free? Is that the kind of country we want for our senior citizens?
There is a plan to switch university students to a voucher system. At present, students can decide whether to study philosophy, history, religion or whatever. They make the decision. They can go to the Canada Student Loan Board and they are entitled to their money. The minute you switch to a voucher system, which is something this Government is actively considering, then the Government can decide to give a grant to someone studying economics but maybe not to someone studying history. That will be Government control over a historic freedom in our society.
We saw this in the oil industry. Prior to the National Energy Program, someone could set up an oil company. He could hire five geologists and drill where he thought there might be oil. He could deduct the cost of that against any revenue from that well. The National Energy Program changed that totally. Now he has to go to Ottawa and establish whether he is "Canadian" or not. If so, he will get a better grant than an entrepreneur from another country. Second, if he wants to drill in Alberta, he may get a 40 per cent grant. The bureaucrats may say that if you go farther and drill on the other side of an imaginary line, your grant will be up to 80 per cent.
That has fundamentally changed the nature of the oil industry from one where people were drilling and competing for oil exports. They now drill federal dry wells on federal lands. That is a waste of money. As a result, the conventional crude in Alberta, which started at 16 billion barrels, went down to 4 billion barrels, is dropping dramatically and will soon be gone. It is not being replaced. I wonder if I might call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: ENERGY-GOVERNMENT COAL PRICING POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT COAL ACREAGE BE RETURNED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
ENERGY-GOVERNMENT COAL PRICING POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT COAL ACREAGE BE RETURNED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 15, 1983,1 asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) to explain what the Government was going to do with the 50,000 acres in coal blocks in southeastern British Columbia now that the Crowsnest rate legislation was being brought in. The price of coal blocks was frozen at $2 per ton for domestic use under the terms of the Crowsnest Agreement. While I agree that it should be free, the Canadian Constitution grants control and ownership of resources to the Provinces.
May 10, 1983

I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to guarantee that the 50,000 acres of land would be returned to the Province of British Columbia. If the Agreement is broken the Province of British Columbia should have the lands turned back to it for development, according to its time schedule. Approaches have been made to the federal Government by various coal companies to develop the property.
What concerns me is that under the terms of the Crowsnest Agreement B.C. Rail will receive up to $635 million per year for the next three years for upgrading of the railway system while its subsidy coal company is applying to the federal Government for the development of these coalfields. I think that is wrong. The Province of British Columbia should have the opportunity of deciding how and when these fields should be developed, not the federal Government.
One of the reasons people in the west feel left out is that agreements such as the Crowsnest Agreement are likely to be broken or changed without their consent. Land should be turned back to whoever owned it when agreements were made between the Provinces and the railways.
I ask the Minister to make a commitment here and now that, if there are to be changes to the Crowsnest agreement, this 50,000 acres with a coal reserve estimated in the neighbourhood of $450 billion will be turned back to the Province. The Minister has stated clearly that the federal Government is the rightful owner of the property and that it would look into the situation if the problem arises. I think that is the attitude that has created the resentment which exists in the West.
I would urge the Minister to consider my comment and look at the very serious problems that will be created for the development of energy in the Province of British Columbia as a result. If Newfoundland has the right to offshore drilling, if Alberta has the right to energy and to set gas prices, surely the Province of British Columbia should have that property turned back to the rightful owner.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-GOVERNMENT COAL PRICING POLICY. (B) REQUEST THAT COAL ACREAGE BE RETURNED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be worthwhile to take a moment to review the history of the Dominion coal blocks. The Government of Canada holds the mineral and surface rights on two tracts of land totalling 50,000 acres, in the Crowsnest Pass coalfield of the Kootenay district in B.C. The Government holds these rights under the Crowsnest Pass Act of 1897. Under this legislation the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was required to carry certain products-including coal and grain-at fixed rates and to grant certain running rights on its railway lines subject to control of the Governor in Council. The Act also conveyed to the federal Government a portion up to the extent of 50,000 acres of any coal-bearing lands granted to the CPR as a subsidy for the construction of the railway by the B.C. Government.
While the Crowsnest Pass Act deals primarily with matters related to railway transportation, particularly those related to the movement of grain, the coal lands are dealt with in sub-
Adjournment Debate
clause l(i) which stipulates that coal be sold at $2.00 or less per ton.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) stated in response to a question raised in the House on March 15, the reason the Government is introducing companion legislation to its Western Grains Transportation Initiatives is to remove the constraints on the exploitation of the Dominion coal blocks, mainly, repealing the Clause limiting the selling price of coal to $2 per tonne.
Historically, Mr. Speaker, there has been some debate between the Government of Canada and the Province of British Columbia as to who controls the coal rights in the Dominion coal blocks. This has hampered development of these resources. From the late 1960s to 1971, licences to explore this coal were granted by the federal Government to four mining companies. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources did not renew these non-exclusive exploration licences in 1971 because of the aforementioned restrictive subclause 1 in the Crowsnest Pass Agreement, and the uncertainty about when such a restriction would be removed. The federal Government's energy policy is aimed at utilizing a rational mix of all the available domestic sources of energy.
In this context, the Government will be increasing its reliance on Canadian coal. Coal reserves in the Dominion coal blocks are considerable. They have been tested for quality and have been determined to be of good metallurgical grade. No serious development of these resources can commence until legal problems are resolved.
This brings us back to the amendments to the original 1897 legislation. The Government is hopeful that Transport Canada's Western Grain Transportation Initiatives legislation is passed through Parliament without any complications or delay, thereby facilitating the Government's expedient resolution of problems impeding, Mr. Speaker, the development of coal in the Dominion coal blocks.

subtopic: TRADE-REQUEST THAT TRADE OFFICES BE ESTABLISHED IN TAIWAN. (B) POSSIBLE SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
TRADE-REQUEST THAT TRADE OFFICES BE ESTABLISHED IN TAIWAN. (B) POSSIBLE SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue I am raising today is based on my questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last week, on May 4, regarding two associated matters; namely, the potential sale of at least one Candu Reactor to Taiwan now, thereby creating some 25,000 jobs in Canada, and second, the need for us to join the rest of the modern world of international trade and commerce and establish a permanent, but non-diplomatic trade office in Taiwan in order to promote Canadian trade with that country.
Let me say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that I was pleased that the Prime Minister did not reject these proposals outright, and in fact said, "If the Hon. Member wants to suggest that I take a trip to Taiwan, I will entertain the suggestion." I do suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister visit Taiwan to

May 10, 1983
Adjournment Debate
see for himself one of the fastest growing economies in the world today. He would also see the tremendous trade potential which Canada and Canadians are missing simply because we do not have any presence whatsoever in that country to promote trade. Yet, and I want to emphasize this, every other non-communist industrialized nation in the world has some form of a trade office in Taiwan, and they are taking advantage of that tremendous growth and potential in international trade in that country. Yet they do it without jeopardizing their diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China. There is no question about it. Sweden was the last western country to open an office in Taiwan just this January. It has not lost one cent of trade with China. It has not jeopardized its diplomatic relations with Red China and it has increased its sales with Taiwan considerably, as have all of the other nations which are based there. Canada and Italy are the only two countries outside the non-communist industrialized world which are not represented there.
Why do I and others advocate such a move? The answer is very simple, Mr. Speaker. It is because international trade creates jobs in Canada. Canadians are today faced with the highest unemployment level in the history of this country and we are missing the boat in international trade, in Taiwan and elsewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE-REQUEST THAT TRADE OFFICES BE ESTABLISHED IN TAIWAN. (B) POSSIBLE SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext: No.

subtopic: TRADE-REQUEST THAT TRADE OFFICES BE ESTABLISHED IN TAIWAN. (B) POSSIBLE SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary says, "no". He is going to read some prepared text, but he does not know what he is talking about. After my seven minutes I will give him a chance.
The United States Department of Commerce, for example, states that for every $1 billion American dollars in exported goods 24,000 indirect and direct jobs are created. Statistics Canada says that for every $1 billion of exported goods and services, 26,123 man-years of direct and indirect employment are created. Because Taiwan is one of the fastest growing economies in the world we must join the rest of the world in promoting Canadian trade abroad.
I was pleased to see that the Prime Minister appeared to be positive in his response, particularly from the quote that I just gave. Following my questions in the House and private meetings with Liberal Members, many of whom are on the Canada-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Committee, as well as in a conversation I had with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), I was assured the Government would be looking toward improving trade relations with Taiwan for the benefit of Canada and Canadians.
It is urgent for Canadian businessmen and Canadians to have two things in Taiwan: a permanent trade office like other countries; and better and more viable travel arrangements, in other words, visa offices where visas are processed. Right now a Canadian businessman has to go to the U.S. in order to obtain a visa to go to Taiwan to do business and sell Canada.
The situation is the same for Taiwanese businessmen who want to come to Canada and buy Canadian, and they do. I am assured they want to buy Candu reactors. We already have one there. The Parliamentary Secretary may not know that, but it is an experimental one being run by the U.S.
Taiwan also needs our high technology because it has one of the fastest growing economies in the world. It is turning from labour intensive industry to high-tech industry. It needs our communications, our transportation equipment and our agricultural know-how, not to mention our raw materials such as coal, sulphur, pulp and paper, potash and so on.
I am delighted that the Prime Minister seemed to be positive. I am delighted that the Minister of Energy was positive in suggesting that such an idea of selling Candus and expanding our trade relations with Taiwan should be pursued. I know the Parliamentary Secretary is now going to read some prepared text about which he knows absolutely nothing, so I will give him the opportunity to do that, and pursue the matter with the Prime Minister and Minister of Energy at a later date.

subtopic: TRADE-REQUEST THAT TRADE OFFICES BE ESTABLISHED IN TAIWAN. (B) POSSIBLE SALE OF CANDU NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
If the Canadian private sector is contemplating doing that, be sure the Government will give it serious consideration. We do not see any obstacle to the establishment in Taiwan of branch of a Canadian organization comparable to these others.
When the Hon. Member talks about selling the Candu, he makes it very simplistic, but it is not like selling a pair of shoes. It has a political dimension which cannot be ignored. The Canadian Government has a policy rooted in serious concerns about nuclear non-proliferation. There is no obvious mechanism for Taiwan's formal compliance with our non-proliferation requirements, namely, the signature of the NPT or an equivalent binding commitment to non-proliferation, or NPT-type full scope safeguards under an agreement with the IAEA, or bilateral agreement with Canada providing for fallbacks,
May 10, 1983

prior consent rights, physical protection and other provisions. Taiwan is not a member of the International Atomic Energy Agency and we cannot, having no diplomatic relations, sign a bilateral safeguards agreement with it. Naturally, it would be desirable if we could resolve such difficulties and sell a superior Canadian product like the Candu, but we must do so with full attention to the political situation and our non-proliferation concerns.
The Hon. Member was giving figures about jobs that are created in Canada by trade. I would like to remind him that if we use his calculations, 31,347 jobs are created by our exports to China. The Hon. Member should know that and take it into consideration. We have many links with that country. We are open to his suggestions, but he must realize that there is no simple answer.

subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-SCHEDULED IMPOSITION OF USER FEES IN ALBERTA. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
MEDICAL CARE-SCHEDULED IMPOSITION OF USER FEES IN ALBERTA. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to follow up on a number of questions I have been asking the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) during the last while concerning her announced intentions last year to bring in a new health act which would consolidate all the existing health care legislation in Canada and at the same time clarify national health care standards in Canada and the five basic principles of medicare.
I am concerned that we have not yet seen the Canada health Act. It apparently is still in the drafting process which has continued now for some time. As a result of this inaction or delay on the part of the federal Government things are proceeding at a pace which constitutes an ever increasing threat to the existence of medicare. I have said before on a number of occasions that it is not any one action by any one Province which can be said to lead to the end of medicare, but the combination of all things that have happened over recent years and months, in particular, which have contributed to a scenario in which we can see ourselves finding medicare, as we have known it and as Canadians have wanted it, being lost.
I urge upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare the concern that what she does or does not do in the near future will be extremely crucial to the future of medicare in this country. She cannot continue only with what has often been acceptable rhetoric and the arguments with which she has come to be identified. I recall as far back as before the 1979 election when she was Minister of National Health and Welfare and came to the rhetorical defence of medicare. I also recall when she was in the Opposition attending a conference on the crisis in medicare at that time.
Since then we have had the health services report which recommended that action be taken with regard to extra billing by physicians. We have also had the special Parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements which took place a year after the Hall Report and which made
Adjournment Debate
recommendations concerning extra billing, and in a number of other areas regarding medicare and the maintenance of national standards. It will be two years this September since that special Parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements made its report.
Alberta introduced a new regime of user fees, this spring. New Brunswick recently announced that it would be bringing in certain user fees for certain hospital services. Last fall we saw the Progressive Conservative Ontario Government initiate a system whereby hospitals are allowed to be run by American multinationals for a share of the profits they can generate by running those hospitals. We believe that to be in violation of the spirit of non-profit administration, one of the five basic principles of medicare.
I could continue with other instances in which the spirit and, indeed, even the letter of medicare are being violated by Provinces. We still have no concrete action on the part of the federal Government regarding a Canada Health Act. I understand how difficult it will be for the federal Government to bring in a Canada Health Act that will address all of these issue in a comprehensive and competent way, but I want the Government to do that, and I want the Government to do something soon in that direction. That is why I have urged the Minister to put a proposal before this House.
The Minister does not seem to have any luck with the Provinces. She has not met with provincial representatives for almost a year now. I do not think we can wait until we finally get around to having another meeting between the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the provincial Ministers of Health. I think what the Minister should do is put her proposal for a Canada Health Act before this House, table it as a white paper, or in whatever form she desires, and let Members of Parliament and the Canadian public respond to it. It will be a good document if it is the kind of proposal around which people can rally, and through which they can put pressure on their respective provincial Governments to come to the bargaining table here in Ottawa and bargain in the interests of medicare, and not just in the narrow fiscal or ideological interests of Progressive Conservative provincial Governments.
In closing, I might add that the federal Government also has a responsibility to act in the interests of medicare, not just in its own fiscal self-interest. It must put some money back on the table. The federal Government has to remedy some of the fiscal injustices it has done to the Provinces in the last year so that it can come to the table and bargain hard and bargain well for the future of medicare.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-SCHEDULED IMPOSITION OF USER FEES IN ALBERTA. (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all aware that Canada's health care system and its health care insurance plans are facing extremely difficult economic times. It is precisely at such times that important programs come under the most stress and risk. We are also all aware of the sources

May 10, 1983
Adjournment Debate
of stress to the health care system. The demands for new health programs, new technology, growth in existing programs, upgrading of existing facilities and equipment, increasing wages and fees are some of these pressures. Perhaps all of them could be solved with a huge increase in revenues to the program, but we all know that this is not an available solution. Where would this money come from? From governments? From the consumers? From both?
It is clear that all sources of revenue are stretched to the limit. However, a wide range of revenue sources is being seriously considered in these times, as we see in the recent budget plans of Alberta and New Brunswick, in spite of long standing federal legislation on medicare.
Unfortunately, program legislation drafted 25 years ago under different fiscal arrangements is simply not well suited to meet the expectations of the public in the 1980s, particularly in light of our economic conditions. Nor does our legislation provide sufficient clarity for the provinces to know just what conditions are still necessary, as a minimum, to qualify for the very substantial contributions to medicare provided by the federal taxpayers.
It was with these stresses and risks in mind, as described by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall in his 1980 report "Canada's National-Provincial Health Program for the 1980's, and by the all party federal Parliamentary Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements in its August, 1981 report, that the Minister met with the provincial health Ministers in May, 1982 to propose the new Canada Health Act.
The Ministers of Health agreed at the meeting that open and co-operative discussions should proceed quickly at both
the ministerial and official levels, to complete discussions as soon as possible on a new Canada Health Act to replace the existing Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the Medical Care Act. The Minister was very pleased that a basic commitment to high quality care and to the principles of universality, portability, comprehensiveness and accessibility of medicare was stressed by all.
The development of new legislation through federal-provincial consultation is a process which should itself facilitate the maintenance of conditions in the 1980s and beyond, because it seeks to arrive at a clear understanding of what Parliament intends to require of a Province in order that transfer funds will be provided for the health insurance program and of what the Provinces are committed to with regard to the medicare program.
I strongly assure the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) that work is progressing systematically and thoroughly on the new Canada Health Act and that as soon as it is appropriate the Minister will be meeting with the provincial health Ministers to complete the consultation process before introducing the new act to Parliament. This is a very important program to Canadians and it is essential that the time be taken to develop the act properly.
